businessProblem: An HR-tech SaaS reads healthy at the top line (35% growth) but is quietly deteriorating underneath: quarterly logo churn doubled (2%→4%), NRR fell from 108% to 101%, and NPS dropped from 38 to 27. The owner attributes this to feature parity and price pressure from larger bundled suites and wants to spend scarce engineering and cash on differentiation and discounting. However, churn exit data, single-module concentration (recruitment 88% vs onboarding 41% and performance 19%), a 47-day time-to-first-value, low QBR completion (38%), and CSM overload (80 accounts each) all point to value-realization and post-sale engagement failures inside the installed base. With ~35% of the base renewing in the next two quarters and 20 months of runway, the owner must decide where to point the next two quarters of capacity before a retention problem becomes a Series B problem.

evidence.finding: Quarterly logo churn rose from 2% to 4% across three consecutive quarters and NRR fell from 108% to 101%. Exit surveys on 22 churned logos cite 'didn't get full value / low adoption' (55%) and 'switched to bundled suite' (23%) far ahead of explicit 'price' (14%). The dominant stated reason is unrealized value inside accounts, not headline competitive loss.
evidence.source: Billing system churn ledger, NRR cohort report, churn exit-survey transcripts

evidence.finding: Adoption is concentrated in one module: recruitment 88%, onboarding 41%, performance 19%; the average account actively uses only 1.4 of 3 modules. Single-module accounts churn at roughly 3x the rate of multi-module accounts in the CS notes, and they generate the expansion shortfall behind the NRR decline. Customers are buying a suite but realizing a point tool.
evidence.source: Product usage analytics, CS account notes

evidence.finding: Time-to-first-value (first hire fully processed) averages 47 days versus a 21-day target. QBR completion is 38%, and each CSM carries ~80 accounts, well above the 40-50 healthy band for this ACV. Accounts that miss early value rarely expand to a second module, and they over-index in the churn cohort.
evidence.source: Onboarding milestone tracker, CS QBR log, CS capacity model

evidence.finding: Two larger HR suites bundle comparable modules at list-price parity and appear in renewal evaluations. Win rate on new business is stable at 24% and sales cycle is unchanged (~70 days), indicating the competitive pressure shows up at renewal/expansion, not at acquisition. This is consistent with a retention/value problem rather than a front-of-funnel competitiveness collapse.
evidence.source: Win/loss notes, competitive renewal evaluations from CS

evidence.finding: Blended CAC rose 15% YoY to ~$22k and CAC payback extended to 19 months (from 14). The payback deterioration is driven more by shrinking NRR/expansion and rising churn (lower LTV per logo) than by acquisition cost alone; the owner's 'unit economics' framing is a downstream symptom of retention decay.
evidence.source: Finance unit-economics model, CAC payback computation
